item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q020_syntaxin_fragment_reclassification","answer":"In current SCOPe release 2.08, the early structures are retained but explicitly qualified as incomplete: d1br0a_ and all three 1ez3 domains (d1ez3a_, d1ez3b_, d1ez3c_) are annotated as “three-helical fragment; similar to one spectrin repeat” and carry the `ms` inconsistency for secondary structures missing from the common domain. They nevertheless share SCCS a.47.2.1 with full-length d1dn1b_: class All alpha (a; SUNID 46456), STAT-like fold (a.47; 47654), t-SNARE superfamily (a.47.2; 47661), and t-SNARE family (a.47.2.1; 47662). Thus the fragment-based assignments should be reinterpreted as partial observations of the Syntaxin 1A N-terminal domain, not as evidence that the complete domain is an autonomous spectrin repeat or that its full architecture and boundaries are captured by the fragments. The spectrin-repeat comparison is local structural resemblance; it does not establish homology to spectrins. Conversely, common t-SNARE family placement is substantially stronger evolutionary evidence among these syntaxin records, while sharing only the broader STAT-like fold with another protein would not by itself establish homology or justify function transfer. Sequence records illustrate the coverage difference: d1br0a_ is 120 residues and d1ez3a_ 124, versus 222 for d1dn1b_. The complete record has no missing-structure flag, but 1dn1 is obsolete and replaced by 3c98; SCOPe classifies d1dn1b_ by an automated match to the nonobsolete full-domain d3c98b_. Therefore fragments remain suitable local templates for their observed helices, but not for whole-domain modeling, domain-boundary inference, conformational-state inference, or detailed interaction/function transfer. For full-domain representation, d3c98b_ is preferable, with the additional caveat that it is observed in a Munc18–syntaxin complex and does not alone represent every biological conformation.","evidence_used":["mcp__scope__get_scop_service_info — /api/v1/;
